newsitem.title: CANADA: Six thousand more workers set to walk out on GM Canada.
newsitem.headline: Six thousand more workers set to walk out on GM Canada.

text.p: About 6,000 General Motors Corp. workers are set this weekend to join 15,000 others on strike in Canada unless the carmaker and the Canadian Auto Workers' union resolve a bitter standoff over shifting work to outside companies.

At 11:59 p.m. EDT on Sunday, unionized workers at GM's St. Catharines, Ontario plant, about 30 miles (48 km) south of Toronto, will walk off the job as part of an escalating strike that will see the entire 26,000-member GM Canada workforce on the picket line by Oct. 9.
The CAW began an escalating strike against GM on Wednesday after failing to convince the company that it should accept a deal patterned on an agreement forged with Chrysler Corp. two weeks ago.

CAW President Buzz Hargrove warned GM that the union was prepared to strike North America's biggest carmaker if it did not reverse decisions on shifting work to outside companies, a practice known as outsourcing, that would cut 5,500 jobs.
"If you think somehow this thing is going to crumble, you have a rude awakening coming as we look to the future," Hargrove said on television as union officials applauded.

He accused company officials of lying to the public about the profitability of a parts plant that GM has put up for sale. He said he would not back down until GM accepted the pattern agreement banning job reductions through outsourcing and a moratorium on the sale or closing of profitable plants.

Hargrove said he met with GM Canada lead negotiator Dean Munger on Friday, but was leaving Toronto for membership meetings across Ontario until Sunday. He said Munger could reach him to continue talks at any time.
Analysts said a strike by all GM union workers in Canada could cost the world's largest automaker $100 million to $150 million a week and eventually force plants to shut down in the United States.

Separate talks continued between GM and the United Auto Workers union in the United States. UAW President Stephen Yokich said the union needs to make strategy decisions of its own and will confer with CAW leaders on how to proceed.
Hargrove said he spoke to Yokich on Thursday and was assured the UAW would not make any moves that would steal bargaining power from the Canadian union.

Hargrove said that in addition to outsourcing -- the use of outside contractors, usually non-union workers -- the two sides remained "worlds apart on hours and work rule issues. He said he believed the Canadian talks were sunk by GM's Detroit headquarters.

Munger said Thursday the strike would have a "severe impact" on GM Canada operations, but declined to speculate when the impact would reach U.S. operations or cripple GM's just-in-time parts supply strategy.
GM said a strike in Canada would not affect talks with the UAW in the United States. "We're working pretty much independently," GM spokesman Gerry Holmes said.

The CAW has said its C$50 million ($36.5 million) strike fund could last up to eight weeks and stretch to 16 weeks if new credit is arranged. The union also has set a special meeting for Oct. 18 to raise funds from all 210,000 members of the CAW.
Economists said a prolonged strike against GM in Canada could hurt the country's economic recovery, shaving up to 1 percentage point off growth in the fourth quarter.
"I think a short strike would have only a transitory effect, but a long one could be very damaging," said John McCallum, chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto.
